honestAccounting: Three of the five planned classes were NOT authored. One (surface.native.op × [env:read, fs:list]) hit the §6 enforcement-defect stop and is filed as issues/20260806-exactwhich-declares-typed-effects-it-never-emits.md. The other two candidate classes at this size — surface.host.abi × [env:read] (6 cells / 30 rows) and surface.startup.env × [env:write] (5 cells / 25 rows) — were assessed and rejected as out of reach in this session: neither has an executor that can produce a source-bound typed-decision receipt for an EFFECTFUL surface of its kind, so both are executor-construction work, not template authoring. That assessment is itself a calibration finding (see costModelFindings).

measuredSlope.caution: DO NOT project the campaign from these two classes. Both are native-op cells with existing executor support and 1–2 cells each. The rows-per-class distribution is extremely skewed (the largest in-scope class is 454 rows across 77 surfaces; these were 6 and 10), and the two classes that would have tested a different surface kind were the ones that turned out to need executor construction. §9's 8-week line cannot be evaluated on this sample.

costModelFindings: LLP 0036's 'authoring a family is nearly free; the cost is a small executor edit per family' is confirmed and refined: BOTH completed classes required a Rust executor change, not just a template. Three distinct executor generalizations were needed for six rows of class 1 alone.

The dominant cost was not template design and not tokens — it was the correction loop, and 3 of the 5 correction-loop iterations were mechanical compile errors from adding a field to a struct with test literals. That is cheap but serial: each iteration costs a full cargo rebuild (20–75 s) plus a catalog regen (11 s).

The batch's loud named failures worked exactly as LLP 0044 predicted. Two of five iterations were real contract mismatches that a hand-authored guess would have papered over: (1) the native executor could not express a denial-return surface at all, (2) a first-principles nine-vs-seven decision-count guess was wrong — the D3 rule earning its keep for the second time in this corpus.

Surface-kind coverage is the binding constraint on calibration, not row count. Only native-op had an executor able to produce an effectful source-bound receipt. surface.host.abi has a probe path, but it admits only NON-CAPABILITY module-runner ABIs with zero expected decisions; surface.startup.env has an effectful probe path, but it is keyed to a closed table of eleven reviewed process.env read sources and its env:write cells are Android/Rust startup sources with no JS-invocable surface at all. A tranche that spans surface kinds must budget executor construction for each new kind.

Two of the ~40 in-scope native-op cells examined carry an effects classification over a LEGACY authorization path that emits no typed decision (__exactWhich via checkCapability, __exactHandleReadFileSync via ex_host_handle_check). If that ratio holds, the campaign should expect a steady trickle of enforcement-defect stops, each of which is a §9 reforecast trigger.
